item.title: Floquet spectra and parameter sensitivity of entanglement in the quantum kicked top
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows for the first time that peaks in entanglement sensitivity of a quantum‑kicked‑top processor line up with Floquet eigenphase degeneracies and short‑period revivals, providing a concrete spectral fingerprint of where small changes in control parameters produce large entanglement swings. By demonstrating that the resultant of the characteristic polynomial can map these “hot spots” even for just four qubits—and arguing that the pattern extends to higher spin values—the work offers a practical diagnostic tool for calibrating chaotic‑type quantum simulators and for tailoring gate sequences that deliberately harness or avoid such sensitivity. In the broader landscape, it bridges the long‑standing gap between quantum chaos theory and near‑term algorithmic design, suggesting new ways to predict error amplification in hardware that exploits periodically driven dynamics.

We investigate the relationship between the Floquet spectrum and the sensitivity of the entanglement landscape to parameter and initial condition change in the quantum kicked top. We focus on the case of four qubits and on locating degeneracies in its Floquet eigenphases using the resultant of its characteristic polynomial $p$ and its derivative $\partial_λp$ and quantitatively map the sensitivity of the entanglement landscape to changes in kicking strength over the sphere of spin coherent initial states. We find that prominent sensitivity maxima coincide with either Floquet eigenphase degeneracies or kick strengths exhibiting short-period quantum revivals, with some points satisfying both conditions. These results establish a connection between the spectral structure of the Floquet operator and entanglement landscape sensitivity, demonstrating the utility of the resultant in studying the dynamics of small-$j$ quantum kicked tops. Since this structure extends to all values of $j$, the central lessons apply completely generally.

item.title: Reducing RSA-2048 Factoring Resources Below One Billion Toffolis via LLM-Driven Verifiable Quantum Compilation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a clever LLM‑guided redesign of the RNS arithmetic pipeline can slash the Toffoli count for Shor’s RSA‑2048 attack to under one billion—a milestone that narrows the gap between theoretical attacks and realistic hardware requirements. By delivering a Pareto frontier of qubit‑Toffoli trade‑offs, it builds on Gidney’s 2025 optimizations and demonstrates that automated code‑generation tools can uncover resource savings that hand‑crafted designs miss. While still far from today’s noisy devices, the result sharpens the timeline for when fault‑tolerant quantum computers could threaten current public‑key infrastructure, underscoring the urgency of post‑quantum migration.

Modular exponentiation dominates the logical cost of factoring 2048-bit RSA integers (RSA-2048) with Shor's algorithm. Recent approaches based on approximate residue number systems (RNS) sharply reduce the required logical qubits, yet still demand billions of Toffoli gates. Optimizing these circuits is difficult because shared ancilla qubits and measurement-based uncomputation tightly couple the arithmetic stages, while rare overflows in compressed registers occur too infrequently for random simulation to detect. Here we use large language model (LLM)-driven search to redesign the RNS pipeline across stages and build a deterministic compiler that produces a Pareto frontier of RSA-2048 circuits. We bound rare overflow probabilities analytically and verify the resulting elementary gate sequences across all constituent RNS primes on representative circuits. Relative to Gidney's 2025 baseline under matched adder accounting, our frontier cuts the minimum qubit-Toffoli product by 70.1% and lowers expected factoring Toffolis by up to 78.6% at matched accumulator precision, bringing RSA-2048 factoring below one billion Toffolis for the first time.

item.title: Resilience of Entangling Gates to Spatiotemporally Correlated Noise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the choice of two‑qubit entangling gate can dramatically affect a processor’s tolerance to the spatially and temporally correlated noise that becomes dominant as devices scale up, identifying CZ and √iSWAP as intrinsically more robust than SWAP in semiconductor spin qubits. By deriving a general filter‑function formalism that maps measured noise spectra onto gate‑specific error budgets, the work provides a practical design rule for hardware engineers seeking to optimise error rates without additional control overhead. The result dovetails with recent efforts to characterise low‑frequency 1/f noise and suggests that careful gate selection could buy valuable fidelity margins even before full error‑correction is deployed.

As quantum processors scale, spatially and temporally correlated noise is emerging as a limiting factor in the fidelity of multiqubit gates. Here we show that this makes the choice of entangling operation a first-order design decision: for two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits, the CZ and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates exhibit a pronounced resilience to correlated noise relative to the SWAP gate, even though correlated fluctuations of the entangling interaction can degrade gate performance to a level comparable to that of local noise. We trace this hierarchy to the redistribution of noise-sensitive channels away from zero frequency and show it to hold for noise spectra dominated by low-frequency weight, including $1/f$ and Lorentzian. These results follow from a general expression, derived here, for the average gate infidelity under arbitrary spatiotemporal noise correlations, valid for generic multiqubit systems and system-environment coupling structures. The infidelity takes the form of a spectral overlap between the noise correlation matrix and a gate-dependent filter function, in which the coherent dynamics of the gate itself shapes the spectral window through which correlated fluctuations enter. The framework converts measured noise correlations into quantitative error budgets and provides a concrete design principle for selecting entangling operations in scalable quantum architectures.

item.title: Solving the Traveling Salesman Problem Using Quantum Devices: QUBO and HOBO Formulations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it tackles one of the most concrete benchmarks for near‑term quantum optimizers—mapping the NP‑hard traveling salesman problem onto hardware‑friendly formulations and quantifying the trade‑off between qubit count and circuit depth. By showing that a higher‑order binary optimization (HOBO) encoding can halve the required qubits compared with the traditional QUBO approach, the authors provide a practical pathway for running larger TSP instances on today’s noisy intermediate‑scale quantum devices using VQE or QAOA. The work also clarifies when the extra gate overhead of HOBO outweighs its qubit savings, giving developers a clear recipe to choose the most realistic formulation for upcoming hardware upgrades.

The traveling salesman problem (TSP) forms the foundation for many logistics and optimization tasks. At the same time, this problem is NP-hard and requires significant computational resources. Quantum computing promises to substantially accelerate computations or increase solution accuracy. The TSP can be conveniently mapped onto the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) formulation, which in turn can be solved using variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) methods, but this mapping requires a quadratic number of qubits. The higher-order binary optimization (HOBO) formulation requires significantly fewer qubits, but it contains higher-order terms. In our work, we thoroughly investigate both formulations and provide a practical recipe for solving the TSP. We give a comprehensive study and compare in detail QUBO and HOBO formulations.

item.title: Linear entanglement suffices for $f$-routing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a lingering open question in quantum communication complexity by proving that any Boolean‑controlled routing task can be achieved with only 2n + 2 EPR pairs, bringing the entanglement requirement down from super‑polynomial to linear for all functions f. By shifting the burden to an exponentially long quantum message from Alice while keeping Bob’s side classical, it highlights a concrete trade‑off between shared entanglement and communication bandwidth that will inform the design of future distributed quantum networks. Although the total resource cost remains higher than earlier schemes when both messages and entanglement are counted, the linear bound sharply limits how much entanglement‑saving lower‑bounds can ever be proved, tightening our theoretical understanding of quantum routing protocols.

In $f$-routing, Alice receives an $n$-bit string $x$ and an unknown qubit, and Bob receives an $n$-bit string $y$. They share a state prepared in advance and exchange one simultaneous message each. The party selected by the Boolean function $f(x,y)$ must then recover the unknown qubit without further communication. To perform $f$-routing successfully, Alice and Bob need to share entanglement that scales with $n$ for some functions $f$, but the lower and upper bounds for the entanglement are not tight. This paper shows that $2n+2$ shared EPR pairs suffice for every function $f$. The best previous bound that holds for all functions is a shared state of $2^{O(\sqrt{n\log n})}$ qubits. The new strategy moves the cost from the shared state to the messages: Alice sends an exponentially long message of $2^{n+1}+1$ qubits, while Bob sends only classical bits. When the messages are counted towards the resources as well, the previous strategy remains the cheapest known. The result also limits lower bounds that count only the shared state: they cannot exceed a linear number of EPR pairs. The result is formalized in Lean.

item.title: Mitigating drift in spin-qubit control with calibration-insensitive pulses
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that silicon‑spin qubits can retain fault‑tolerant gate fidelities for days using calibration‑insensitive pulse shapes, eliminating the labor‑intensive retuning that has long hampered quantum‑dot scaling. By demonstrating that adiabatic BIR‑4 and composite CORPSE pulses stay within 99 %–99.97 % Clifford fidelity despite large power or frequency drifts, the work bridges a gap between laboratory‑grade control and the robust, low‑maintenance operation required for industrial‑scale processors. The results dovetail with recent efforts in pulse engineering and automated calibration, suggesting that hardware‑level drift mitigation may become a standard tool as silicon spin qubits move toward commercial foundry production.

Silicon spin qubits offer fault-tolerant control fidelities in a platform that is compatible with commercial foundries, but device calibration drifts and control parameters must be retuned every few hours. Here, we replace conventional square control pulses with two drift-resilient pulse families: the adiabatic BIR-4 and the composite CORPSE. In a Si/SiGe quantum-dot device, we benchmark single-qubit gate sets built from each pulse against deliberate miscalibration. We find that BIR-4 offers a 99% Clifford fidelity over a factor of 2 change in drive power and CORPSE maintains similar fidelity over +/-0.9MHz of offset. When fully calibrated CORPSE offers a 99.97% fidelity per gate, on par with a calibrated square pulse. Starting with tuned pulses, we then track errors using gate-set tomography for ten days without recalibration. BIR-4 holds its rotation angle to 0.3 degrees throughout, including across a 1.3MHz frequency jump. Our results demonstrate that these pulses can maintain high-fidelity operations without constant recalibration, mitigating the need for constant tuning, which is a key bottleneck in scaling quantum-dot-based quantum processors.

item.title: Optimal fidelity over zero-capacity erasure channels
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing question about how well quantum information can survive through zero‑capacity erasure channels by giving an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity in the antidegradable regime. By leveraging fractional extendibility to prove a tight upper bound and then constructing permutation‑invariant codes that meet it, the authors demonstrate that even “useless” channels can preserve nontrivial quantum coherence when used with suitably tailored error‑correcting schemes. The result sharpens our theoretical limits for quantum networking over highly lossy links and informs the design of practical codes that approach these limits in future quantum repeaters.

Antidegradable quantum channels have zero capacity for reliable quantum communication. However, they can nevertheless transmit quantum information with nontrivial fidelity. This raises the question: how well can quantum information be preserved through such channels? In this work, we exactly characterize the optimal asymptotic entanglement fidelity of quantum erasure channels throughout the antidegradable regime. Specifically, we show that it equals $γ+\frac{1-γ}{d}$ for transmission probabilities $0<γ\le \frac{1}{2}$ and logical dimension $d$. We use fractional extendibility to establish an upper bound on the entanglement fidelity achievable by arbitrary error-correcting protocols. Furthermore, we construct a family of permutation-invariant codes that asymptotically saturates this bound.

item.title: Quantum resources constrain function approximation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints exactly which quantum resources—coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic—are needed to faithfully approximate a given function, moving beyond the generic claim that quantum models are universal approximators. By deriving tight bounds for one‑ and two‑qubit circuits and showing how Clifford‑only training can recover uniform approximation with only polynomial depth overhead, it connects directly to current efforts to design hardware‑efficient quantum machine‑learning algorithms for noisy intermediate‑scale devices. The work clarifies when exotic resources such as non‑Clifford “magic” actually boost accuracy, giving practitioners a concrete guide for matching circuit resources to the structure of their target functions.

Universal function approximation is central to machine learning. Quantum learning models are universal as well, but this does not specify the resources needed to approximate a given function. We study how coherence, imaginarity, entanglement and magic constrain function approximation for a fixed encoding and readout, using the cumulative resource power of the trainable gates. In a one-qubit model with phase encoding, coherence bounds the oscillation of the model function, while imaginarity bounds its odd part. In a two-qubit model, entanglement bounds the distance from product functions. These bounds hold at any encoding depth. For magic, the phase encoding itself supplies non-Clifford operations. On domains bounded away from zero, Clifford trainable gates suffice for uniform approximation. Replacing unrestricted trainable gates by Clifford gates increases the encoding depth at most polynomially in the original depth, the inverse error and the inverse distance of the domain from zero. Magic in the trainable gates can nevertheless improve accuracy at fixed depth. These results show how the resources of a quantum model must match the structure of the target function.

item.title: Optimizing Locally Equivalent Graph States in Quantum Computing Using Greedy Best-First Search
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a simple greedy best‑first search can systematically locate locally equivalent graph states with far fewer edges than previously achievable, directly cutting the number of costly CZ gates and circuit depth needed for measurement‑based quantum computing and repeater networks. By framing the local‑complementation problem as a state‑space search, the authors outperform heavyweight integer‑linear‑programming and local‑search methods across random, bounded‑degree, and LDPC‑derived graphs—an advance that could ease hardware constraints on connectivity and error‑rate budgets. The work also highlights that escaping early local minima is essential, suggesting future algorithmic refinements may further tighten resource overheads for large‑scale quantum architectures.

In measurement-based quantum computation and quantum repeater networks, graph-structured quantum states called graph states play a central role as an essential resource. In a graph state, each vertex corresponds to a qubit, and each edge is prepared by applying one controlled-Z (CZ) gate. Local complementation, which toggles adjacencies among the neighbors of a selected vertex, produces operationally equivalent graph states up to an inexpensive operation called local Clifford gates. Therefore, finding equivalent graphs up to local complementation with fewer edges and lower maximum degree can reduce the preparation cost, such as the number of CZ gates and the circuit depth. In this paper, we formulate the problem of finding a desirable equivalent graph via local complementations as a state space search problem. We apply a heuristic search algorithm, greedy best-first search (GBFS), to the formulated problem. Our experimental evaluation shows that despite its simplicity, GBFS outperforms existing approaches based on integer linear programming or local search across multiple graph classes, including random graphs, bounded-degree graphs, and most of the graphs constructed from quantum LDPC codes. In addition, we empirically analyze GBFS's search behavior, confirming that we need search rather than stopping at the first local minimum to find the best solution.

item.title: THeatA: Transport- and Heating-aware QEC simulation with Cooling Strategies for QCCD Trapped-Ion Systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces THeatA, a full‑stack simulation framework that explicitly tracks ion‑by‑ion motional heating during transport and schedules cooling operations, allowing realistic error models for QCCD trapped‑ion processors. By linking the mean phonon number to gate‑dependent error rates, it reveals how shuttling‑induced heating can dominate logical error scaling of surface‑code cycles—information that was missing from prior QEC simulators. The work arrives as several groups are prototyping modular ion traps, giving them a practical tool to balance transport speed, cooling overhead, and fault‑tolerance thresholds. Its current focus on single‑species linear arrays means further extensions will be needed for mixed‑species or two‑dimensional architectures.

The quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) architecture is a promising approach to scalable trapped-ion quantum computing, enabling flexible qubit interactions by transporting ions between dedicated trap zones. Programs for such systems require operations beyond conventional circuit primitives: ion shuttling, physical SWAPs, trap splitting and merging, and cooling. Motional excitation accumulated during transport increases the mean phonon number of ions and degrades the fidelity of the two-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates. However, existing quantum error correction (QEC) simulation frameworks do not jointly track per-ion motional excitation and explicitly schedule cooling operations with their transport time and heating costs. We develop a full-stack software framework for QEC experiments and simulations on linear QCCD systems with a single ion species, comprising an intermediate representation (IR) supporting QCCD-native operations, a compiler that translates syndrome-extraction circuits into the IR, and a heating-aware noise-injection pipeline that generates noisy Stim circuits. The compiler updates the mean phonon number of each ion throughout the schedule, and the pipeline derives gate-dependent error rates from the tracked phonon states and per-ion timing, enabling the evaluation of finite-size logical-error scaling of the rotated surface code under transport- and heating-aware noise. We show that transport-induced heating prevents logical error rates from decreasing with increasing code distance under the evaluated conditions, and that indirectly cooling the ion pairs involved in two-qubit gates, by merging them with precooled coolant ions immediately before each gate, restores this decrease. By sweeping the duration and post-cooling mean phonon number of an abstract cooling instruction, we characterize their trade-off and identify the region in which logical-error scaling is maintained.

item.title: Quantifying superposition via coherence by stochastic orthogonalization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first operational bridge between the abstract notion of quantum superposition and the well‑studied resource theory of coherence, showing that stochastic orthogonalization measurements can convert any superposition into a quantifiable amount of coherence. By defining a “degree of superposition” that inherits the operational meaning of existing coherence measures, it offers a practical tool for benchmarking how much useful interference a hardware platform or sensor can actually generate. The work also clarifies fundamental limits—such as why deterministic conversion to maximally coherent states is only possible for up to three reference states—informing both theoretical resource‑theory research and the design of devices that rely on precise superposition control.

Here we present an approach to quantifying superposition of nonorthogonal reference states through quantum coherence. No change of basis achieves this: every orthonormal basis makes some superposition-free states appear coherent. We show that orthogonalization succeeds instead as a measurement mapping every reference state onto a multiple of a basis vector in each outcome; such measurements are exactly the free operations that convert superposition into coherence. The largest average coherence they extract from a state, which we call its degree of superposition, turns every coherence measure into a superposition measure with the same operational meaning. An interference term becomes coherence at most with the probability of unambiguously discriminating its two reference states, a bound attained when there are no others and, for positive coefficients and nonnegative overlaps, exactly when the overlaps are probabilities of a random grouping. Maximal degree means conversion into a maximally coherent state with certainty, possible for up to three reference states but not in general. Each coherence measure gives its own degree; when two degrees order two superpositions oppositely, neither converts into the other with certainty, and we find such pairs already for two reference states, unlike in qubit coherence. For equal positive overlaps, in-phase superpositions are rigid: deterministic conversions that keep all components can only permute their coefficients. As the reference states merge, the degree stays bounded where widely used measures can diverge, and at every amplitude a rotation-symmetric cat state attains its maximum. Our results quantify superposition operationally and reveal conversion constraints created by nonorthogonality.

item.title: Quantum Cyclic XYZ Stabilizer Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a new family of cyclic XYZ stabilizer codes that extend the familiar CSS construction by incorporating Y‑type checks, and it shows how assigning disjoint irreducible factors of \(x^n\!-\!1\) yields explicit codes with provably optimal distances for a given length and dimension. By proving that these codes achieve minimum distances beyond the best known CSS bounds—and even surpass linear‑programming limits—the work demonstrates that non‑CSS, highly symmetric stabilizers can deliver stronger error protection without sacrificing the regular structure prized by hardware designers. The result dovetails with recent pushes toward more versatile fault‑tolerant architectures, suggesting a practical pathway to higher‑performance quantum memories and logical gates built on cyclic, easily implementable circuits.

XYZ codes generalize the Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) framework by adding $\sym{Y}$-type stabilizers to the usual $\sym{X}$- and $\sym{Z}$-type ones. We study XYZ codes whose three classical component codes are binary cyclic codes of odd length~$n$. Assigning disjoint sets of irreducible factors of $x^n-1$ to the three Pauli types fixes the number of encoded logical qubits and ensures that the row spaces of the three parity-check matrices intersect pairwise trivially. Then, a coprimality condition between the factors assigned to each type and the reciprocals of those assigned to the others guarantees the required orthogonality. Cyclotomic cosets give a complete and explicit description of the resulting family. We show that, for odd~$n$, a cyclic stabilizer code admits an XYZ representation with cyclic component codes iff its stabilizer generators are invariant, up to a phase, under the qubit permutation $i\mapsto 2i\bmod n$. By fixing the length and the dimension of the code, the proposed cyclic XYZ codes attain the best known minimum distance of stabilizer codes, exceed the minimum distance of the underlying CSS codes, and even exceed the linear-programming upper bounds for general CSS codes.

item.title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum $k$-Cut Problem
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a binary‑tree variant of QAOA that tackles the Max‑k‑Cut problem with only 2k – 3 MaxCut subproblems, dramatically cutting qubit and gate counts compared with conventional k‑level encodings. By showing that the approximation ratio degrades only modestly across successive splits, the authors provide a theoretical guarantee that the method scales gracefully on noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices—a key hurdle for applying QAOA to real‑world combinatorial tasks. The work therefore broadens the practical reach of variational algorithms, offering near‑term hardware users a more resource‑efficient pathway to solve multi‑partition graph problems without sacrificing solution quality.

The maximum $k$-cut (Max-$k$-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the $k$ possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with $k$. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-$k$-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most $2k-3$ subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after $k-1$ steps form an approximate solution to the Max-$k$-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.

item.title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the often‑assumed “uniform photon‑loss” model can break down when a weakly nonlinear bosonic mode couples to spectrally engineered noise, causing loss rates that depend on the Fock state and pushing logical information outside the intended error space. By demonstrating both the transient non‑Markovian dynamics and the eventual convergence to a Markovian limit in a 3D circuit‑QED platform, the work connects directly to recent advances in cat‑ and binomial‑code experiments that rely on precise dissipation engineering. The findings warn designers of bosonic error‑correction schemes that realistic, state‑dependent environments must be included in noise budgets if scalable fault tolerance is to be achieved.

Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory. By applying narrowband noise to a binomially encoded logical qubit, we further demonstrate Fock-state-dependent dissipation channels that drive logical states beyond the nominally correctable error space. These results establish structured environmental noise as a mechanism for deforming photon-loss errors in weakly nonlinear bosonic systems and highlight the need to incorporate realistic, state-dependent dissipation into the design and characterization of bosonic quantum error correction.

item.title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article presents the first quantum algorithms that can prepare low‑temperature thermal states of impurity models with polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and only polylogarithmic dependence on precision, eliminating the exponential β overhead that has limited previous Gibbs samplers. By enabling efficient ground‑state and finite‑temperature simulations of the core building blocks of dynamical mean‑field theory, the work brings quantum advantage for studying strongly correlated materials within reach. The Heisenberg‑limited estimation of static and dynamical properties further shows that practical material‑science calculations could soon benefit from near‑term quantum processors, provided the impurity Hamiltonian has a suitable spectral gap.

Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

item.title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints exactly how much expressive power remains in a quantum neural network when the measurement operator is locked by hardware, showing that unitary, mixed‑unitary and general CPTP dynamics form three strictly nested families of reachable observables. By mapping these families to concrete geometric objects—a fixed‑spectrum orbit, its convex hull and an operator interval—the work gives designers a clear checklist for what can (and cannot) be learned without adding trainable readout layers, a question that has become urgent as near‑term devices are increasingly constrained by fixed detectors or sensor architectures. The derived loss floors also provide the first quantitative benchmarks for how much error mitigation or ancillary channels are needed to reach full CPTP expressivity, guiding both algorithm developers and experimentalists toward more realistic quantum‑ML pipelines.

A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

item.title: 500 Hz atom-atom entanglement distribution over metropolitan-scale fibers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a semi‑deterministic entanglement link that pushes the distribution rate past half a kilohertz across a 20 km fiber span—an order of magnitude faster than any prior single‑ or two‑photon scheme and achieved without active phase stabilization. By combining two 15×15 quantum‑memory arrays, the researchers show how multiplexing can simultaneously deliver high efficiency and robustness, directly addressing the bottleneck that has limited practical quantum repeaters. The result sets a new speed benchmark for metropolitan‑scale quantum networks and brings scalable, fault‑tolerant architectures one step closer to real‑world deployment, though extending the technique to longer distances and integrating it with error‑corrected nodes will be the next challenge.

Quantum networks and repeaters are among the most promising routes to scale up quantum information systems. Nevertheless, various aspects still require significant improvement to achieve practical realization. Multiplexing can enhance the performance in many fundamental steps, thus emerging as a critical strategy for the realization of quantum repeaters. Currently, a major bottleneck in realizing functional quantum repeaters is heralded entanglement distribution over longdistance elementary links, as neither of the two dominant protocols-single-photon nor two-photon interference-can simultaneously achieve high efficiency and strong robustness. Here, we address this challenge by experimentally realizing a method that unifies the efficiency and robustness. By harnessing two 15 * 15 quantum memory arrays, we generate remote matter-matter entanglement at a rate of 546 Hz over 20 km of fiber without active phase stabilization. This rate exceeds that of two-photon and single-photon schemes by factors of 75,932 and 23, respectively, establishing a new benchmark for entangling speed over metropolitan-scale distances and enabling semi-deterministic entanglement distribution. Inherently compatible with multiplexed quantum repeater architectures, our scheme offers a promising approach towards the realization of future high-performance distributed quantum systems.

item.title: Complex chaotic Boltzmann machines as deterministic representations of quantum states
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine can encode any pure quantum state as a deterministic trajectory in a high‑dimensional hypercube, extending the neural‑network wavefunction paradigm to a fully dynamical representation that captures both Born probabilities and relative phases. By turning the variational parameters of a network into the geometry of regular curves, islands and unstable regions, it offers a fresh way to visualise and explore phase information that is usually hidden in standard neural‑quantum‑state approaches—a capability that could sharpen variational algorithms and state‑tomography techniques. The work builds on recent successes of neural quantum states and tensor networks, but its reliance on low‑dimensional examples means further scaling studies will be needed before it can impact large‑scale quantum simulations.

Neural networks and tensor networks have opened new ways to explore quantum systems by parameterizing families of wave functions through the structure and parameters of a network. Here we extend this perspective to a dynamical representation: we introduce a complex chaotic Boltzmann machine that assigns a deterministic system to a pure quantum state. We extend Suzuki's construction to incorporate both Born probabilities and relative phases. The probabilities set the trajectory velocities in a hypercube, while the phases define a complex field that lifts its Poincare sections. The evolution is determined by the network parameters and initial conditions, without random choices during flights or configuration changes. Our analysis of two qubits and study of three-qubit families show how relations between probabilities organize regular curves, islands, and unstable regions, and how phases distinguish states that share the same Born dynamics. This architecture turns a wave-function parameterization into a geometry of trajectories, providing a tool to explore probabilities, phases, and symmetries together across families of states.

item.title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a long‑standing obstacle for quantum annealers—efficiently handling linear constraints without inflating the problem into dense penalty graphs that quickly outstrip the sparse connectivity of current superconducting chips. By exploiting single‑shot spin‑fluctuation covariances to reconstruct dual curvature, the SelfCal‑QSQN scheme eliminates extra slack qubits and penalty couplers, enabling full‑chip feasibility on D‑Wave Advantage devices and delivering performance that rivals time‑matched mixed‑integer solvers at the 256‑spin scale. The result opens a realistic pathway for applying quantum annealing to real‑world constrained optimization in finance, power grids and logistics, though further work will be needed to confirm scalability beyond today’s few‑hundred‑qubit problems.

Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

item.title: Detection of genuine multipartite entanglement by means of entanglement monotones
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a systematic way to construct genuine multipartite‑entanglement monotones that can certify “irreducible” D‑partite entanglement—states that cannot be broken down into lower‑order pieces—a capability that has been missing from most existing measures. By showing that no entropy‑based witness can satisfy both LOCC‑monotonicity and subadditivity, the authors motivate a relaxed LO‑monotone approach that nonetheless succeeds in detecting any form of genuine tripartite entanglement in three‑qubit systems, offering a powerful new benchmark for emerging quantum processors. The result dovetails with recent efforts to develop hardware‑friendly entanglement diagnostics and could help validate multi‑qubit gates and error‑correction codes once experimental protocols are built around these monotones.

We look for pure state entanglement monotones that may serve as certificates of a strong form of genuine multipartite entanglement, that we refer to as irreducible entanglement: a $D$-partite state (with $D\geq 3$) is irreducibly $D$-partite entangled if it cannot be decomposed as a product of states that are at most $(D-1)$-partite entangled. We start by establishing a no-go result proving that no reasonable genuine multipartite entanglement entropy can simultaneously obey LOCC-monotonicity and subadditivity. After relaxing the first condition to LO-monotonicity, we provide a simple method generating genuine multipartite entanglement monotones with the desired properties. Focusing on a subfamily of these monotones, we show that they are able to detect any form of genuine tripartite entanglement in three-qubit systems.

item.title: Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first ancilla‑free construction of exact Dicke‑state circuits that reaches both optimal linear gate count and logarithmic depth for any Hamming weight, a milestone because Dicke states are key resources for quantum metrology, error‑correcting codes and variational algorithms. By disproving the previously conjectured Ω(k) depth bound for balanced Dicke states, it shows that large‑scale symmetric entanglement can be generated far more efficiently than thought, opening the door to near‑term hardware demonstrations on modest qubit arrays. The constant‑time amplitude‑amplification step also means the method scales cleanly without costly iterative subroutines, although practical performance will still depend on native two‑qubit gate fidelity and connectivity. Readers should watch how this technique is adopted in quantum sensing prototypes and as a building block for more complex state‑preparation pipelines.

We construct exact circuits for $n$-qubit Dicke states of any Hamming weight $k$ using $O(n)$ single-qubit gates and CNOTs in $O(\log n)$ depth without ancillary qubits. The gate count and depth are asymptotically optimal for every $0<k<n$. We compress symmetric blocks to free output qubits for weight-dependent phases. A sign correction followed by a collective rotation produces a state whose overlap with the target is at least a positive constant, so exact amplitude amplification takes $O(1)$ steps. For balanced Dicke states ($k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$), the logarithmic depth disproves the $Ω(k)$ depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang (2025).

item.title: Quantum control of an electrically levitated nanoparticle with a trapped ion
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single laser‑cooled ion can act as a quantum “refrigerator” and control hub for an electrically levitated nanoparticle, opening a realistic path to ground‑state cooling and non‑Gaussian state engineering of macroscopic objects. By exploiting parametric modulation of the Paul‑trap potential to resonantly enhance Coulomb coupling, the scheme builds on recent hybrid ion–nanoparticle experiments and complements optomechanical approaches that rely on optical tweezers, offering a fully electrical route with potentially lower photon‑scattering heating. If experimentally realized, such ion‑nanoparticle hybrids could become versatile testbeds for macroscopic quantum physics, precision sensing, and even modular quantum networking, although achieving the required trap stability and mitigating charge noise will be critical challenges.

Quantum control of levitated nanoparticles offers a route towards macroscopic quantum states. Here we propose a novel way to achieve it for a nanoparticle levitated electrically in a linear Paul trap together with a single ion, a system recently realized experimentally. By suitably engineering the trap's AC potential, one can parametrically modulate the ion-nanoparticle distance and thus the Coulomb coupling to enable a resonant interaction. For realistic parameters, we calculate that this enables sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle to its motional ground state by a single, continuously laser-cooled ion. Additional AC drives enable the preparation of squeezed nanoparticle states and of ion-nanoparticle entanglement. Moreover, non-Gaussian states such as Fock and cat states, prepared in the ion with standard trapped-ion techniques, can be transferred to the nanoparticle with high fidelities. We provide complete protocols for each of these states, including all known decoherence sources. Our results establish electrically trapped ion-nanoparticle systems as a platform for quantum control of levitated matter.

By showing how identical topics can play very different pedagogical roles depending on their contextual framing, the study offers educators concrete guidance for designing courses that bridge mathematical rigor, experimental intuition, and computational relevance—a need sharpened by the rapid expansion of quantum‑technology programs worldwide. The roadmap also gives institutions a practical tool for selecting or adapting textbooks to produce graduates who can more readily transition into research labs or industry teams building real quantum hardware.

Instruction in quantum mechanics (QM) is often categorized by its entry point as 'wave-first' or 'spin-first', yet these labels lack consistent definitions and overlook other established or emerging approaches. Moreover, while capturing broad differences in topic selection and sequencing, this binary framing obscures critical differences in contextualization--how three dimensions (mathematical tools, phenomena and experiments, and theoretical concepts) are framed and connected to support student sensemaking. Research also rarely examines how such pedagogical choices unfold across the undergraduate-to-graduate trajectory. Using textbooks as an analytical lens to map these choices and characterize overarching pathways, encompassing entry points and overall orientations, we comparatively analyze the selection, sequencing, and contextualization of core topics across these 3 dimensions, alongside prefaces and introductions, in 36 university QM textbooks spanning countries and eras. At the topic level, we show that identical topics occupy widely different curricular roles depending on their contextualization. Synthesizing these findings into pathways, we identify three additional entry-point archetypes (labeled path-, qubit-, and axiom-first) and characterize all 5 approaches, showing that most textbooks combine multiple archetypes in their opening chapters. Extending this synthesis beyond entry points, we map textbooks' overall orientations relative to mathematics, experiment and application, and theoretical physics. Interpreting these profiles alongside authors' rationales reveals how educators navigate competing trade-offs among mathematical accessibility, theoretical generality, physical motivation, and modern developments. This study provides a multidimensional framework, substantive examples, and a practical roadmap for textbook selection and curriculum design in QM education.

item.title: Classical simulability and hardware diagnostics for QAOA on geographic coverage benchmarks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a carefully crafted classical reference can expose hidden shortcomings in QAOA performance, revealing that the modest energy reductions observed on a 24‑qubit device are largely reproduced by an uncorrelated product distribution rather than genuine quantum correlations. By demonstrating that a larger, exactly simulable 51‑qubit encoding preserves the problem’s structure while remaining tractable blockwise, the work provides a practical diagnostic toolkit for distinguishing true algorithmic progress from artefacts of benchmark design. The approach builds on recent efforts to benchmark variational algorithms with realistic hardware constraints and offers a concrete method for researchers to validate whether observed improvements reflect quantum advantage or merely statistical noise. It cautions practitioners that without such diagnostics, optimistic claims about QAOA scalability could be misleading.

Quantum-optimization benchmarks can show reduced energy while concealing local loss of weighted covariance. We combine encoding checks with exact structural references to select informative circuit diagnostics for static geographic coverage instances. The executed 24-qubit surrogate has infeasible ground states, whereas a faithful 51-qubit slack encoding preserves its 13 support-graph components and remains exactly simulable blockwise. At the executed angles, the total ideal optimum probability is $5.47\times10^{-20}$, making optimum counts uninformative at the executed budget of $10^5$ shots. A product distribution with the measured bit marginals accounts for about $90\%$ of the observed energy reduction. In three fixed-circuit jobs, the global weighted-covariance ratio is approximately $0.50$, while a five-variable block has ratios between $0.12$ and $0.28$ and contributes only $3.7\%$ of the ideal global denominator. Simultaneous bands resolve its deficit relative to the global ratio under an exploratory conditional counting model. The exact block reference thus reveals a local discrepancy concealed by the aggregate, without identifying an error mechanism or establishing device stability. The procedure links benchmark structure to the resolution and limitations of its observables.

item.title: Practical insights into controlling exponential concentration in quantum machine learning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles the “exponential concentration” bottleneck that has been limiting the scalability of quantum machine‑learning models, a problem closely related to the barren‑plateau phenomenon identified in recent variational‑circuit studies. By systematically comparing fidelity‑based kernels, projected kernels and quantum extreme learning across locality, entanglement and circuit depth, the authors show that bandwidth scaling can temper concentration in moderately expressive regimes, offering a practical knob for designers of near‑term QML algorithms. The work therefore provides concrete guidance on how to balance encoding expressivity against measurement sensitivity, an insight that will be valuable as researchers move from proof‑of‑concept kernels toward larger, hardware‑friendly quantum learning pipelines.

Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models are often limited by exponential concentration, where quantum observables become insensitive to input variations as system size increases. In this work, we provide a comparative empirical study of this phenomenon across Fidelity Quantum Kernels (FQK), Projected Quantum Kernels (PQK), and Quantum Extreme Learning (QEL), within a unified observable-based framework based on expectation-value variance. We investigate how measurement locality, entanglement, and circuit expressivity shape concentration across different architectures. Global fidelity-based kernels exhibit strong concentration driven by Hilbert space dimensionality, whereas local-observable approaches reduce but do not eliminate this effect. In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

item.title: Quantum-Chaos-Assisted Measure Synchronization in a Double-Well Ultracold Bose Gas
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that quantum chaotic dynamics can dramatically accelerate measure synchronization in a double‑well Bose‑Einstein condensate, revealing a direct link between chaos, rapid synchronization and high entanglement entropy. The finding suggests a new route for fast state preparation or stabilization in analog quantum simulators, complementing recent advances in Floquet engineering and dissipative control of many‑body systems. Nonetheless, the results are derived from an idealized two‑mode Josephson model, so extending chaos‑assisted synchronization to larger, noisy platforms will require additional experimental and theoretical work.

This paper investigates measure synchronization (MS) in a two-component ultracold atomic system confined in a double-well potential, which realizes a quantum many-body bosonic Josephson junction. Through spectral-statistics analysis, we identify the quantum chaotic parameter regime and confirm that the system achieves MS within this regime with weak dependence on the initial energy imbalance. We further show that chaotic dynamics not only significantly shortens the time scale for establishing synchronization but is also accompanied by entanglement entropy approaching the random-state prediction. These results reveal close connections among quantum chaos, MS, and quantum entanglement in conservative quantum many-body systems and may motivate further studies on the underlying mechanisms of chaos-assisted synchronization.
